blocks.x: Chapter 8 ended with a promise, that \(x^2+7x+12\) equals \((x+3)(x+4)\). Multiply to check. \((x+3)(x+4)=x(x+4)+3(x+4)=x^2+4x+3x+12=x^2+7x+12\), so the promise holds. An expression \(ax^2+bx+c\) with \(a\) not zero is a quadratic. This lesson multiplies linear factors into quadratics. Reversing that is the next lesson's job.
Multiply \((x+5)(x+6)\) the way the opener multiplied its product, splitting the first factor and distributing each part over the second. Collect like terms and enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Write the product as \(x(x+6)+5(x+6)\). That is chapter 2's distributive property with the whole factor \((x+6)\) as the multiplier.
Each part distributes again, four products in all. Two of them contain \(x\) to the first power, and those two collect.
blocks.sol: \((x+5)(x+6)=x(x+6)+5(x+6)=x^2+6x+5x+30=x^2+11x+30\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{11}\). The two cross products \(6x\) and \(5x\) are like terms, and collecting them is where the middle term of every such product comes from.

blocks.x: Expand \((x+10)(x-2)\), keeping the minus sign with the \(2\) in both products that use it. Enter the constant term of the result.
hints: Split as \(x(x-2)+10(x-2)\) and distribute each part. Two of the four products come out negative.
The constant term is the product of the two constants, \(+10\) and \(-2\), sign included.
blocks.sol: \((x+10)(x-2)=x^2-2x+10x-20=x^2+8x-20\), so the constant term is \(\boxed{-20}\). The only constant is \(10\cdot(-2)\), negative because exactly one of the two constants is negative.

blocks.x: Distribute twice. \((x+r)(x+s)=x(x+s)+r(x+s)\), the whole second factor treated as a single multiplier, and then each part is distributed again, \(x^2+sx+rx+rs\). Four products in all, every term of the first factor times every term of the second, then like terms are collected. Nothing here is new. Chapter 2's distributive property is used twice, once with \((x+s)\) as the multiplier and once inside each part, and the same two steps apply unchanged for any signs and for any coefficients on \(x\).
Expand \((x-5)(x-8)\). Both constants are negative this time, so all four sign decisions in the four products matter. Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Split as \(x(x-8)-5(x-8)\) and distribute each part, keeping every sign.
The two cross products are \(-8x\) and \(-5x\). The last product, \((-5)(-8)\), is positive.
blocks.sol: \((x-5)(x-8)=x^2-8x-5x+40=x^2-13x+40\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{-13}\). Both cross products are negative and add, while the constant \((-5)(-8)=40\) comes out positive.

blocks.x: Expand \((8x-5)(2x+9)\). The \(x^2\) coefficient is now a product of two numbers, and two of the four products contain \(x\) to the first power. Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Distribute twice as before, \(8x(2x+9)-5(2x+9)\), and write all four products before collecting anything.
The two \(x\) products come from \(8x\cdot 9\) and \(-5\cdot 2x\). Compute both, signs included, then add.
blocks.sol: \((8x-5)(2x+9)=16x^2+72x-10x-45=16x^2+62x-45\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{62}\). With leading coefficients the middle is no longer a plain sum of the two constants, it is \(72-10\), one cross product at a time.

blocks.x: The forward pattern. \((x+r)(x+s)=x^2+(r+s)x+rs\). The two cross products are \(sx\) and \(rx\), like terms, so the middle coefficient is the sum \(r+s\) and the constant is the product \(rs\). Check the first problem, \(5+6=11\) and \(5\cdot 6=30\). The pattern holds for any signs, but only when the \(x^2\) coefficient is \(1\). With leading coefficients the middle was \(72x-10x\), one cross product at a time, not a plain sum. This is a fact about multiplying. Recovering \(r\) and \(s\) from an expansion is the next lesson's work.

blocks.cap: The rectangle's width is \(a+b\) and its height is \(c+d\), so its area is \((a+b)(c+d)\). The four cells have areas \(ac\), \(bc\), \(ad\) and \(bd\), and they tile the rectangle exactly, so \((a+b)(c+d)=ac+ad+bc+bd\). Every term of one factor multiplies every term of the other, the same four products that appear in the double distribution.

blocks.x: A few products come up so often they are worth knowing on sight, a sum squared, a difference squared, and a sum times the matching difference. Squaring means multiplying by itself, so \((x+k)^2\) means \((x+k)(x+k)\), four products again, and it is not \(x^2+k^2\). The next two problems work out two of these, and the third follows the same way.
Write \((x+8)^2\) as \((x+8)(x+8)\), the square written out as the product it abbreviates, and expand it with the same double distribution as every product so far. Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Squaring means multiplying by itself, so the same double distribution applies, four products again.
The cross product is \(8x\) both times, and the two copies are like terms.
blocks.sol: \((x+8)^2=(x+8)(x+8)=x^2+8x+8x+64=x^2+16x+64\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{16}\). The cross product appears twice, which is why the answer is \(16\) and not \(8\), and why \((x+8)^2\) is not \(x^2+64\).

blocks.x: Compute \(61\times 59\) without a calculator by writing it as \((60+1)(60-1)\) and expanding all four products. Enter the product.
hints: The four products are \(60\cdot 60\), \(60\cdot(-1)\), \(1\cdot 60\), and \(1\cdot(-1)\). Two of them cancel.
The cross products are \(-60\) and \(+60\), so they add to zero. You are left with one square minus a much smaller square.
blocks.sol: \(61\times 59=(60+1)(60-1)=3600-60+60-1=3600-1=\boxed{3599}\). The cross products cancel whenever the two factors are the same distance from a round number, one above and one below, which is what makes this a mental calculation.

blocks.x: Three named identities. \((a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\), \((a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2\), and \((a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2\), the difference of squares. Each one is the same double distribution. The difference square is \((a-b)(a-b)=a^2-ab-ab+b^2\), the cross product \(-ab\) twice, and the sum square is the same with \(+ab\), the source of the \(16\) in \((x+8)^2\). In the conjugate product the cross products are opposite and cancel, which is why \(61\times 59\) reduced to \(3600-1\). The middle term of a square is \(2ab\), not \(ab\), and a middle term is missing only in the conjugate product.

An expansion is a claim that the two sides are equal at every value of \(x\), so they must agree at any value you try. At \(x=10\), \((x+1)(x+8)\) is \(11\cdot 18=198\), and \(x^2+9x+8\) is \(100+90+8=198\). At \(x=0\) only the constant term is left, so pick a nonzero value. Agreement at one value is strong evidence. A disagreement proves an error.
A student expands \((x+6)(x+9)\) and writes \(x^2+14x+54\). Substitute \(x=10\) into the product and into the claim to confirm they disagree, then enter the correct coefficient of \(x\).
hints: At \(x=10\) the product is \(16\cdot 19\). Evaluate the claim at \(10\) as well and compare.
The constant \(54\) is correct, since \(6\cdot 9=54\). Recompute the two cross products, \(9x\) and \(6x\).
blocks.sol: At \(x=10\) the product is \(16\cdot 19=304\) while the claim gives \(100+140+54=294\), so the claim is wrong. Expanding correctly, \((x+6)(x+9)=x^2+9x+6x+54=x^2+15x+54\), and the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{15}\). The gap between \(304\) and \(294\) is \(10\), exactly one missing \(x\) at \(x=10\).

blocks.x: The acronym FOIL, First Outer Inner Last, first appeared in William Betz's 1929 textbook Algebra for Today. The label is centuries younger than the method, and the method needs no acronym, it is the distributive property used twice.
Expand \((x-10y)(x+8y)\). The same rule applies, every term of the first factor times every term of the second, with two letters to track. Enter the coefficient of \(xy\).
hints: Four products again, \(x\cdot x\), \(x\cdot 8y\), \(-10y\cdot x\), and \(-10y\cdot 8y\). Two of them contain both letters.
Collect \(8xy\) and \(-10xy\). The \(y^2\) product is separate and is not the answer.
blocks.sol: \((x-10y)(x+8y)=x^2+8xy-10xy-80y^2=x^2-2xy-80y^2\), so the coefficient of \(xy\) is \(\boxed{-2}\). The \(xy\) coefficient is the collected sum \(8-10\), while \(-80\) is the \(y^2\) coefficient, the product.

blocks.x: The zero product property. If a product of two numbers is zero, then at least one of the numbers is zero. The reason is short. The product of two nonzero numbers is never zero, so if a product is zero there is no other possibility. The consequence is the whole point of factored form. An equation with a product on one side and zero on the other splits into separate linear equations, one for each factor, and solving linear equations is chapter 4's work.

The payoff is immediate. In \((x-6)(x+10)=0\) a product equals zero, so at least one factor is zero, and each factor gives a chapter 4 equation. \(x-6=0\) gives \(x=6\), and \(x+10=0\) gives \(x=-10\), the sign flipped. Of the two, \(6\) is the larger, since \(-10\) is negative. A factor can also be \(x\) itself, and \(x=0\) is already solved.
Solve \((x-8)(x+15)=0\). The left side is zero exactly when one of the factors is zero. Enter the larger of the two solutions.
hints: Set each factor equal to zero and solve the two linear equations separately.
\(x+15=0\) is solved by a negative number. Compare the two solutions on the number line before choosing the larger.
blocks.sol: \(x-8=0\) gives \(x=8\) and \(x+15=0\) gives \(x=-15\), so the larger solution is \(\boxed{8}\). The factor \(x+15\) is zero at \(-15\), not \(15\), and \(8\gt -15\) even though \(15\) is bigger than \(8\).

blocks.x: The left side of \(x(x-16)=0\) has \(x\) itself as a factor. Count every value of \(x\) that makes the left side zero, then enter the number of solutions of the equation.
hints: The zero product property applies to any two factors. Set each of the two factors equal to zero.
The equation \(x=0\) is already solved, and its solution counts.
blocks.sol: The factors are \(x\) and \(x-16\), so \(x=0\) or \(x=16\), and the number of solutions is \(\boxed{2}\). Dropping \(x=0\) is the common error, but zero is a solution, since substituting it back gives \(0\cdot(0-16)=0\).

blocks.x: At most two solutions. Each linear factor is zero at one number, so two factors give at most two solutions, and a repeated factor like \((x-k)^2=0\) gives exactly one, since both factors are zero at the same number. The property also has a boundary. \((x-a)(x-b)=10\) determines neither factor, because two numbers can multiply to \(10\) in endless ways, \(2\cdot 5\), \(20\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\), and on forever. Only a zero product forces a factor to be zero, so before any splitting the equation must have zero on one side.

Multiplying two binomials is now mechanical, four products and a collection, the same every time. The chapter's prize is the reverse direction, starting from \(x^2+bx+c\) and recovering the factors, because the zero product property applies only to factored form. That reversal starts in the next lesson.
Solve \((10x-25)(2x+1)=0\). Each factor is zero at its own value of \(x\), and neither value is an integer this time. Enter the positive solution as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Each factor gives one linear equation, \(10x-25=0\) and \(2x+1=0\). Solve both.
One solution is negative. The other comes out as a fraction that is not yet in lowest terms, so reduce it before entering.
blocks.sol: \(10x-25=0\) gives \(x=\tfrac{25}{10}=\tfrac{5}{2}\), and \(2x+1=0\) gives \(x=-\tfrac{1}{2}\), so the positive solution is \(\boxed{\tfrac{5}{2}}\). Lowest terms means dividing out the common factor of \(25\) and \(10\), which is \(5\).

blocks.x: There is one value of \(b\) for which \(36x^2+bx+121\) is exactly the square \((6x-11)^2\). Expand the square and compare the two expressions term by term. Enter \(b\).
hints: Use the square-of-a-difference identity with \(6x\) as the first term and \(11\) as the second.
The middle term of the expansion is \(-2\cdot 6x\cdot 11\). Match it against \(bx\).
blocks.sol: \((6x-11)^2=36x^2-2\cdot 6\cdot 11\,x+121=36x^2-132x+121\), so matching middle terms gives \(b=\boxed{-132}\). The standard misses are \(-66\), forgetting the \(2\) in \(2ab\), and \(+132\), dropping the sign of the subtraction.

blocks.x: Every product \((x+r)(x+s)\) expands to \(x^2+(r+s)x+rs\), the sum in the middle and the product at the end. Lesson 9.2, Factoring \(x^2+bx+c\), starts from the expanded form and recovers \(r\) and \(s\), a search with exactly two clues, the sum and the product.

review.x: Expand \((x+1)(x+9)\). Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Distribute twice, \(x(x+9)+1(x+9)\), four products in all.
The two cross products are \(9x\) and \(1x\). Collect them.
review.sol: \((x+1)(x+9)=x^2+9x+x+9=x^2+10x+9\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{10}\).

review.x: Expand \((x-1)(x+14)\). Enter the constant term.
hints: Keep the minus sign with the \(1\) in both products that use it.
The constant term is the product of the two constants, \(-1\) and \(+14\).
review.sol: \((x-1)(x+14)=x^2+14x-x-14=x^2+13x-14\), so the constant term is \(\boxed{-14}\). The sign comes from \((-1)\cdot 14\), one negative constant.

review.x: Expand \((x-2)(x-9)\). Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: All four products still appear. Decide the sign of each one before collecting.
The cross products are \(-9x\) and \(-2x\), and the constant \((-2)(-9)\) is positive.
review.sol: \((x-2)(x-9)=x^2-9x-2x+18=x^2-11x+18\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{-11}\). Two negative constants give a negative middle and a positive constant.

review.x: Expand \((2x+1)(5x+8)\). Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Distribute \(2x\) over the second factor, then \(1\) over the second factor, four products in all.
The two \(x\) products are \(2x\cdot 8\) and \(1\cdot 5x\). Add them.

review.x: Expand \((x+11)^2\). Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Write it as \((x+11)(x+11)\) first. The cross product appears twice.
The middle term of a squared sum is twice the cross product, here \(2\cdot 11\cdot x\).
review.sol: \((x+11)^2=x^2+2\cdot 11x+121=x^2+22x+121\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{22}\). The middle is \(2ab\), not \(ab\), because the cross product appears twice.

review.x: Expand \((x-10)^2\). Enter the constant term.
hints: Use the square-of-a-difference identity with \(x\) and \(10\), or multiply \((x-10)(x-10)\) out.
The constant term is \((-10)\cdot(-10)\), sign included.
review.sol: \((x-10)^2=x^2-20x+100\), so the constant term is \(\boxed{100}\). The constant of a square is always positive, only the middle term carries the minus.

review.x: Compute \(85\times 75\) in your head by writing it as \((80+5)(80-5)\). Enter the product.
hints: This is a sum times the matching difference, so the cross products cancel.
What remains is \(80^2-5^2\).

review.x: Expand \((x+20)(x-20)\). Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: This is a sum times the matching difference. Write all four products before collecting.
The cross products are \(-20x\) and \(+20x\).
review.sol: \((x+20)(x-20)=x^2-20x+20x-400=x^2-400\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{0}\). The expansion has no \(x\) term at all, which is the difference of squares pattern.

review.x: Expand \((2x-9)(8x-1)\). Enter the coefficient of \(x\).
hints: Four products, and every one of them needs a sign decision before you collect.
The \(x\) products are \(2x\cdot(-1)\) and \((-9)\cdot 8x\). Both are negative.
review.sol: \((2x-9)(8x-1)=16x^2-2x-72x+9=16x^2-74x+9\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{-74}\). The constant \((-9)(-1)=9\) is positive while both cross products are negative.

review.x: A student expands \((x+6)(x+10)\) and writes \(x^2+16x+66\). Substitute \(x=5\) into the product and into the claim to see they disagree, then enter the correct constant term.
hints: At \(x=5\) the product is \(11\cdot 15\). Evaluate the claim at \(5\) too.
The middle coefficient \(16\) checks out, since \(6+10=16\). The constant should be the product of \(6\) and \(10\).
review.sol: At \(x=5\) the product is \(11\cdot 15=165\) while the claim gives \(25+80+66=171\), so the claim is wrong. The constant is \(6\cdot 10=60\), so the correct constant term is \(\boxed{60}\). A check at \(x=0\) would have caught this even faster, since substituting \(x=0\) leaves only the constant term.

review.x: Expand \((x-6y)(x+15y)\). Enter the coefficient of \(xy\).
hints: Four products, two of which contain both letters. Collect those two.
The \(xy\) products are \(15xy\) and \(-6xy\). The \(y^2\) product is separate.
review.sol: \((x-6y)(x+15y)=x^2+15xy-6xy-90y^2=x^2+9xy-90y^2\), so the coefficient of \(xy\) is \(\boxed{9}\).

review.x: Solve \((x-13)(x+6)=0\). Enter the larger solution.
hints: A product is zero exactly when a factor is zero. Set each factor to zero.
Each factor's solution has the opposite sign of the constant inside it.
review.sol: \(x-13=0\) gives \(x=13\) and \(x+6=0\) gives \(x=-6\), so the larger solution is \(\boxed{13}\).

review.x: Solve \((x+16)(x+21)=0\). Both solutions are negative. Enter the larger one.
hints: Set each factor to zero. Both solutions come out negative.
On the number line, the larger of two negative numbers is the one closer to zero.
review.sol: The solutions are \(x=-16\) and \(x=-21\), and \(-16\gt -21\), so the larger solution is \(\boxed{-16}\). Larger means further right on the number line, not bigger digits.

review.x: Solve \(x(2x-15)=0\). Enter the positive solution as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The two factors are \(x\) and \(2x-15\). Each gives one linear equation.
One solution is \(0\), which is not positive. Solve \(2x-15=0\) for the other.
review.sol: \(x=0\) or \(2x-15=0\), which gives \(x=\tfrac{15}{2}\), so the positive solution is \(\boxed{\tfrac{15}{2}}\). Zero is a solution too, just not the positive one.

review.x: How many solutions does \((x-17)^2=0\) have? Enter the count.
hints: Write the left side as \((x-17)(x-17)\). Both factors are zero at the same number.
The two factors give the same equation, \(x-17=0\).
review.sol: Both factors are \(x-17\), so the only solution is \(x=17\), and the count is \(\boxed{1}\). A repeated factor gives one solution, not two, since both linear equations are the same.

review.x: To solve \((x-1)(x+13)=10\), Mara sets \(x-1=10\) and answers \(x=11\). Evaluate \((x-1)(x+13)\) at \(x=11\). Enter the value you get.
hints: Substitute \(11\) into each factor separately, then multiply.
At \(x=11\) the second factor is not \(1\), so the product is not \(10\).
review.sol: At \(x=11\) the factors are \(10\) and \(24\), so \((x-1)(x+13)=10\cdot 24=\boxed{240}\). Many pairs of numbers multiply to \(10\), so \(x-1=10\) was only a guess. Splitting an equation factor by factor is valid only when the other side is \(0\).

review.x: Find the value of \(b\) that makes \(81x^2+bx+25\) exactly \((9x-5)^2\).
hints: Expand \((9x-5)^2\) with the square-of-a-difference identity, first term \(9x\), second term \(5\).
The middle term of the expansion is \(-2\cdot 9x\cdot 5\). Match it against \(bx\).
review.sol: \((9x-5)^2=81x^2-2\cdot 9\cdot 5\,x+25=81x^2-90x+25\), so \(b=\boxed{-90}\). Forgetting the factor \(2\) gives \(-45\), and dropping the subtraction's sign gives \(+90\), the two standard misses.

blocks.x: Every product \((x+r)(x+s)\) expands to \(x^2+(r+s)x+rs\), so factoring \(x^2+bx+c\) means finding two numbers with sum \(b\) and product \(c\). Those are the two clues, and the product is the sharper one, since \(c\) has only finitely many factor pairs, so the search starts there.
Two numbers have sum \(15\) and product \(56\). The product is the clue to search on, so list the factor pairs of \(56\) and check each pair's sum. Enter the larger of the two numbers.
hints: Starting from the product gives a shorter search. Only four pairs of whole numbers multiply to \(56\), so list those pairs.
The pairs are \(1\cdot 56\), \(2\cdot 28\), \(4\cdot 14\) and \(7\cdot 8\). Check each sum against \(15\).
blocks.sol: The factor pairs of \(56\) are \(1\cdot 56\), \(2\cdot 28\), \(4\cdot 14\) and \(7\cdot 8\), with sums \(57\), \(30\), \(18\) and \(15\), so the numbers are \(7\) and \(8\), and the larger is \(\boxed{8}\). Starting from the product kept the search short, since only four pairs needed checking.

blocks.x: Factor \(x^2+8x+12\) as \((x+r)(x+s)\). Both constants are positive, since the product and the sum are both positive. Enter the larger of the two.
hints: Two numbers with sum \(8\) and product \(12\). Run the factor pairs of \(12\).
The pairs of \(12\) are \(1\cdot 12\), \(2\cdot 6\) and \(3\cdot 4\). One sum is \(8\).
blocks.sol: The pairs of \(12\) have sums \(13\), \(8\) and \(7\), so the numbers are \(2\) and \(6\), giving \(x^2+8x+12=(x+2)(x+6)\), and the larger constant is \(\boxed{6}\). Expanding back gives \(x^2+8x+12\), the check from 9.1.

blocks.x: The search. To factor \(x^2+bx+c\), find two numbers \(r\) and \(s\) with \(r+s=b\) and \(rs=c\). Then \(x^2+bx+c=(x+r)(x+s)\), which is 9.1's forward pattern read right to left. Run the search through the factor pairs of \(c\), never through sums. There are endlessly many ways to write \(b\) as a sum, but \(c\) has only finitely many factor pairs, so listing the pairs of \(c\) and checking each pair's sum always finishes.

Factor \(x^2+3x-28\). The product of the two constants is \(-28\), so they have opposite signs, and since the sum is \(+3\), the positive one is larger in size. Search the pairs of \(28\) with opposite signs. Enter the negative constant.
hints: You need a factor pair of \(28\) whose difference is \(3\), with signs chosen so the sum comes out positive.
The pairs of \(28\) are \(1\cdot 28\), \(2\cdot 14\) and \(4\cdot 7\). Which pair has difference \(3\)?
blocks.sol: The pair with difference \(3\) is \(4\) and \(7\), and the sum must be \(+3\), so the positive number is \(7\), giving \(x^2+3x-28=(x+7)(x-4)\), and the negative constant is \(\boxed{-4}\). A quick expand gives \(7x-4x=3x\) and \(7\cdot(-4)=-28\), matching the middle term and the constant.

blocks.x: Factor \(x^2-13x+22\). The product \(+22\) is positive, so the two constants share a sign, and since the sum \(-13\) is negative, that shared sign is negative. Search the factor pairs of \(22\), both taken negative. Enter the smaller of the two constants.
hints: \(22\) has only two factor pairs, \(1\cdot 22\) and \(2\cdot 11\), and both numbers are negative here.
Which pair, made negative, sums to \(-13\)? Then take the one farther below zero.
blocks.sol: The negative pairs are \(-1,-22\) with sum \(-23\) and \(-2,-11\) with sum \(-13\), so \(x^2-13x+22=(x-2)(x-11)\), and the smaller constant is \(\boxed{-11}\). Writing \((x+2)(x+11)\) is the standard slip, since its expansion has \(+13x\), not \(-13x\).

blocks.x: Sign reasoning. Both sign facts follow from the forward pattern. A positive \(c\) means \(r\) and \(s\) share a sign, and the sum of two numbers with the same sign has that sign too, so the shared sign is the sign of \(b\). A negative \(c\) means \(r\) and \(s\) have opposite signs, and the sum of two numbers with opposite signs has the sign of the one with the larger absolute value, so that number and \(b\) share a sign. Either way the signs are known before any list gets written, and half the candidate pairs never need checking.

blocks.cap: The rectangle from 9.1, read the other way. Its four cells hold the expansion, \(x^2\), \(rx\), \(sx\) and \(rs\), and the gold side lengths \(x+r\) and \(x+s\) are what factoring recovers. The inside of the rectangle is the expanded form, the sides are the factors, and both clues are visible here, the cross cells add up to \(bx\) and the corner cell is \(c\).

blocks.x: The expansion \(x^2+(r+s)x+rs\) has leading coefficient \(1\), so the two clues are only trustworthy on a quadratic whose \(x^2\) coefficient is also \(1\). Before any search, pull out the greatest common numeric factor and write it in front, where it stays. When there is no constant term, \(x\) itself is a common factor.

Every term of \(4x^2+52x+120\) is divisible by the same number. Pull out that greatest common numeric factor, leaving a quadratic whose \(x^2\) coefficient is \(1\), then finish the factoring. Enter the numeric factor you pulled out.
hints: Find the largest number that divides \(4\), \(52\) and \(120\) evenly.
After it comes out, the search runs on \(x^2+13x+30\).
blocks.sol: The greatest common factor of \(4\), \(52\) and \(120\) is \(\boxed{4}\). It comes out first, leaving \(x^2+13x+30\), which factors as \((x+3)(x+10)\), so the full form is \(4(x+3)(x+10)\), with the \(4\) kept in front.

blocks.x: \(x^2-14x\) has no constant term, so both terms share the factor \(x\) itself. Factor the expression as \(x\) times a linear factor. Enter the constant inside the linear factor.
hints: Write each term with an \(x\) pulled out, \(x\cdot x\) and \(x\cdot(-14)\).
The factorization is \(x(x+s)\) for one value of \(s\), and expanding it must give back \(-14x\).
blocks.sol: \(x^2-14x=x(x-14)\), so the constant inside the linear factor is \(\boxed{-14}\). Expanding back gives \(x\cdot x-14\cdot x\), the original expression.

blocks.x: Common factor first, every time. A quadratic whose \(x^2\) coefficient is \(1\) is called monic, and the two clues are the coefficients of a monic quadratic only. With a leading coefficient still in place, the constant term is no longer plainly \(rs\), so the clues cannot be trusted until the common numeric factor comes out. A missing constant term means every term shares an \(x\), which comes out the same way and is zero at \(x=0\), a root worth keeping once the lesson turns to equations. Skipping this first step is the most common practical error in factoring.

When \(b=0\) the sum clue is \(r+s=0\), so \(s=-r\) and the product is \(-r^2\). That is why \(x^2-49\) factors as \((x+7)(x-7)\), the conjugate identity from 9.1 run backwards, with the cross terms cancelling. The marks to recognize are a missing middle term and a negative perfect square constant.
Compute \(53^2-47^2\) without working out either square. The difference of squares pattern applies to plain numbers too, and it turns the subtraction into one easy multiplication. Enter the value.
hints: The conjugate identity from 9.1, \(a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)\), applies with \(a=53\) and \(b=47\).
blocks.sol: \(53^2-47^2=(53-47)(53+47)=6\cdot 100=\boxed{600}\). Running the identity in reverse replaced two squarings and a subtraction with one easy product, and the direct arithmetic agrees, \(2809-2209=600\).

blocks.x: In 1977 Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman built RSA encryption on a lopsided fact. Multiplying two enormous numbers is quick, but no fast method is known for recovering the factors from the product. Much of internet security rests on that gap.

The quadratic \(x^2+18x+81\) is the search's \(r=s\) case, since \(81=9^2\) and \(18\) is twice \(9\), so it factors as \((x+9)^2\). Now change the constant to \(82\). Run the full search for \(x^2+18x+82\) and answer yes or no. Does it factor with integer constants?
hints: Both numbers would have to be positive, since the sum and the product are both positive. List every factor pair of \(82\).
\(82=1\cdot 82=2\cdot 41\), and those are all the pairs. Check both sums against \(18\).
blocks.sol: The pairs of \(82\) are \(1\cdot 82\) and \(2\cdot 41\), with sums \(83\) and \(43\), and negative pairs have negative sums, so the search comes up empty and the answer is \(\boxed{\text{no}}\). An empty search is a proof, since the pairs are all there is to check.

blocks.x: Two shortcuts and one honest limit. A missing middle term with a negative square constant means a difference of squares, \(x^2-k^2=(x+k)(x-k)\). A constant that is a perfect square, with \(b\) twice its root, means a perfect square trinomial, the \(r=s\) case of the search, \(x^2+2kx+k^2=(x+k)^2\). And because \(c\) has finitely many factor pairs, an empty search is a proof, not a failure. When every pair is checked and none has sum \(b\), no integer factorization exists. Quadratics like that are handled in chapter 11.

Once the left side of \(x^2+bx+c=0\) is factored, it is a product equal to zero, and by the zero product property from 9.1 at least one of the factors is zero. Each factor set to zero is a linear equation. The property applies to a product equal to zero and nothing else, so put zero on one side before splitting anything.
Solve \(x^2-4x-45=0\). Factor the left side, then the zero product property splits the equation into two linear ones. Enter the positive root.
hints: Two numbers with product \(-45\) and sum \(-4\). The signs differ, and the negative one is larger in size.
The pair is \(-9\) and \(5\), so the factors are \(x-9\) and \(x+5\).
blocks.sol: \(x^2-4x-45=(x-9)(x+5)\), so \(x=9\) or \(x=-5\), and the positive root is \(\boxed{9}\). Checking, \(81-36-45=0\).

blocks.x: Solve \(x(x+5)=24\). The left side is already factored, but the right side is not zero, so neither factor is forced to equal anything. Expand, move every term to one side, and factor again before splitting. Enter the positive root.
hints: The zero product property only works on a product equal to zero. Expand and subtract \(24\) first.
\(x^2+5x-24=0\) needs two numbers with sum \(5\) and product \(-24\).
blocks.sol: Expanding gives \(x^2+5x-24=0\), which factors as \((x+8)(x-3)\), so \(x=-8\) or \(x=3\), and the positive root is \(\boxed{3}\). The check runs against the original equation, \(3\cdot 8=24\). Splitting \(x(x+5)=24\) into \(x=24\) or \(x+5=24\) is exactly the trap 9.1 named.

blocks.x: The full pipeline. Rearrange until one side is zero. Pull out the common numeric factor, and \(x\) itself if there is no constant term. Run the search on the monic quadratic that remains, signs settled first. Split with the zero product property. Then check one root in the original equation, the habit from 9.1. Substituting \(x=3\) into \(x(x+5)=24\) gives \(3\cdot 8=24\), the original statement back again, so the pair was right.

You can now factor any quadratic that turns into \(x^2+bx+c\) once a numeric factor comes out, whenever an integer pair exists, and solve the equations built from those factorizations. Two things are still out of reach, a leading coefficient that does not divide out, and a quadratic whose search comes up empty.

A poster is \(6\) inches taller than it is wide, and its area is \(187\) square inches. Writing \(w\) for the width gives \(w(w+6)=187\). Rearrange, factor and split. Both roots solve the equation, but only one can be a width. Enter the width in inches.
hints: Expand and move \(187\) over, then search for two numbers with sum \(6\) and product \(-187\).
blocks.sol: \(w^2+6w-187=0\) factors as \((w+17)(w-11)\), so \(w=-17\) or \(w=11\), and a width is a positive length, so the width in inches is \(\boxed{11}\). The check is the original statement, \(11\cdot 17=187\), an \(11\) by \(17\) inch poster.

blocks.x: Factor \(3x^2-45x+150\) completely. The common numeric factor comes out first. The quadratic left behind has a positive constant and a negative middle term, so both constants in its factored form are negative. Enter the smaller of the two.
hints: Divide \(3\) out of every term, then search \(x^2-15x+50\) among negative pairs only.
Which factor pair of \(50\), both taken negative, sums to \(-15\)?
blocks.sol: Pulling out \(3\) leaves \(x^2-15x+50\), and the negative pair with sum \(-15\) and product \(50\) is \(-5\) and \(-10\), so \(3x^2-45x+150=3(x-5)(x-10)\), and the smaller constant is \(\boxed{-10}\). Dropping the \(3\) when writing the complete factorization is the standard slip, it stays in front.

blocks.x: Every quadratic here began monic or became monic after a numeric factor came out. When the leading coefficient stays, as in \(2x^2+7x+3\), the sum and product clues are no longer enough on their own. Lesson 9.3, Factoring \(ax^2+bx+c\), extends the search to that case.

review.x: Two numbers have sum \(16\) and product \(39\). Enter the larger one.
hints: Search the factor pairs of \(39\). There are only two.
\(39=1\cdot 39=3\cdot 13\). Check both sums.
review.sol: The factor pairs of \(39\) have sums \(40\) and \(16\), so the numbers are \(3\) and \(13\), and the larger is \(\boxed{13}\).

review.x: Factor \(x^2+10x+16\). Enter the smaller of the two constants in the factored form.
hints: Sum \(10\), product \(16\), both constants positive.
The pairs of \(16\) are \(1\cdot 16\), \(2\cdot 8\) and \(4\cdot 4\).
review.sol: The pair with sum \(10\) is \(2\) and \(8\), so \(x^2+10x+16=(x+2)(x+8)\), and the smaller constant is \(\boxed{2}\).

review.x: Factor \(x^2+15x+36\). Enter the larger of the two constants in the factored form.
hints: Sum \(15\), product \(36\), both positive.
Run \(1\cdot 36\), \(2\cdot 18\), \(3\cdot 12\), \(4\cdot 9\), \(6\cdot 6\) and check the sums.
review.sol: The pair with sum \(15\) is \(3\) and \(12\), so \(x^2+15x+36=(x+3)(x+12)\), and the larger constant is \(\boxed{12}\).

review.x: Factor \(x^2+2x-48\). The two constants in the factors differ in sign. Enter the negative one.
hints: Since the product is \(-48\), the signs are opposite, and since the sum is \(+2\), the positive number is larger in size.
You need a factor pair of \(48\) with difference \(2\).
review.sol: The pair of \(48\) with difference \(2\) is \(6\) and \(8\), with the \(8\) positive, so \(x^2+2x-48=(x+8)(x-6)\), and the negative constant is \(\boxed{-6}\).

review.x: Factor \(x^2-12x+35\). Both constants are negative. Enter the smaller of the two.
hints: Positive product, negative sum, so search the pairs of \(35\) both taken negative.
\(35=1\cdot 35=5\cdot 7\). Which negative pair sums to \(-12\)?
review.sol: The negative pair with sum \(-12\) is \(-5\) and \(-7\), so \(x^2-12x+35=(x-5)(x-7)\), and the smaller constant is \(\boxed{-7}\).

review.x: Factor \(7x^2+42x+35\) completely, pulling out the greatest common numeric factor first. Enter the larger of the two constants in the factored form.
hints: Find the largest number dividing \(7\), \(42\) and \(35\) evenly, and take it out before any search.
After it comes out, the search runs on \(x^2+6x+5\), sum \(6\) and product \(5\).
review.sol: The common factor is \(7\), and pulling it out leaves \(x^2+6x+5=(x+1)(x+5)\), so \(7x^2+42x+35=7(x+1)(x+5)\) and the larger constant is \(\boxed{5}\). Without the pull the search on \(7x^2\) never even starts, since the pattern needs a plain \(x^2\).

review.x: Factor \(x^2-22x\) as \(x\) times a linear factor. Enter the constant inside the linear factor.
hints: There is no constant term, so \(x\) itself is the common factor.
The form is \(x(x+s)\), and expanding must give \(-22x\) back.
review.sol: \(x^2-22x=x(x-22)\), so the constant inside the linear factor is \(\boxed{-22}\).

review.x: \(x^2-225\) fits the form \(x^2+bx+c\) with \(b=0\) and \(c=-225\). Factor it as \((x+k)(x-k)\) and enter the positive integer \(k\).
hints: You need two numbers whose product is \(-225\) and whose sum is \(0\).
A pair with sum \(0\) is a number and its opposite, so each one squares to \(225\).
review.sol: The pair must multiply to \(-225\) and add to \(0\), so it is \(15\) and \(-15\), giving \(x^2-225=(x+15)(x-15)\) and \(k=\boxed{15}\).

review.x: Compute \(29^2-21^2\) in your head, as a difference times a sum. Enter the value.
review.sol: \(29^2-21^2=(29-21)(29+21)=8\cdot 50=\boxed{400}\). The sum does not have to be a power of ten for the shortcut to be quick.

review.x: \(x^2-32x+256\) is a perfect square trinomial, \((x+r)^2\) for one value of \(r\). Enter \(r\), sign included.
hints: The constant is a perfect square and the middle coefficient is twice its root, up to sign.
\(256=16^2\) and the middle term is negative.
review.sol: \(256=16^2\) and \(-32\) is twice \(-16\), so \(x^2-32x+256=(x-16)^2\) and \(r=\boxed{-16}\). This is the search's \(r=s\) case, the pair \(-16\) and \(-16\).

review.x: Does \(x^2-7x-44\) factor with integer constants? Run the factor pairs of \(44\) with opposite signs and answer yes or no.
hints: Negative product means opposite signs, and a sum of \(-7\) means the negative number is larger in size.
The pairs of \(44\) are \(1\cdot 44\), \(2\cdot 22\) and \(4\cdot 11\). Check the differences against \(7\).
review.sol: The pair with difference \(7\) is \(4\) and \(11\), with the \(11\) negative, so \(x^2-7x-44=(x-11)(x+4)\), and the answer is \(\boxed{\text{yes}}\).

review.x: Solve \(x^2-3x-70=0\). Enter the larger root.
hints: Two numbers with product \(-70\) and sum \(-3\), so opposite signs with the negative one larger in size.
The pair is \(-10\) and \(7\).

review.x: Solve \(x^2=8x+65\). Move every term to one side before factoring. Enter the negative root.
hints: The zero product property needs zero on one side, so rearrange to \(x^2-8x-65=0\) first.
Two numbers with sum \(-8\) and product \(-65\).
review.sol: Rearranging gives \(x^2-8x-65=0\), which factors as \((x-13)(x+5)=0\), so \(x=13\) or \(x=-5\), and the negative root is \(\boxed{-5}\). Checking in the original, \(25=-40+65\).

review.x: Solve \(x^2=19x\). Do not divide both sides by \(x\), since a root is lost that way. Enter the smaller root.
hints: Move everything to one side, then \(x\) itself is the common factor.
\(x(x-19)=0\) splits into two equations, one for each factor.
review.sol: \(x^2-19x=0\) factors as \(x(x-19)=0\), so \(x=0\) or \(x=19\), and the smaller root is \(\boxed{0}\). Dividing by \(x\) at the start loses exactly this root.

review.x: Solve \(3x^2+27x+42=0\). Pull out the common factor first. Both roots are negative. Enter the larger one.
hints: Dividing out \(3\) leaves \(x^2+9x+14=0\).
The pair for sum \(9\) and product \(14\) is \(2\) and \(7\), and the larger of two negatives is the one closer to zero.
review.sol: Dividing out \(3\) gives \(x^2+9x+14=(x+2)(x+7)=0\), so \(x=-2\) or \(x=-7\), and the larger root is \(\boxed{-2}\). On the number line \(-2\) is to the right of \(-7\).

review.x: Two pages of a book have consecutive page numbers that multiply to \(306\). Consecutive numbers give \(n(n+1)=306\). Solve it, reject the root that cannot be a page number, and enter the smaller page number.
hints: Expand to \(n^2+n-306=0\) and search for two numbers with sum \(1\) and product \(-306\).
The quadratic has one positive root and one negative root, and only the positive one can be a page number.
review.sol: \(n^2+n-306=0\) factors as \((n+18)(n-17)\), so \(n=17\) or \(n=-18\), and a page number is positive, so the pages are \(17\) and \(18\) and the smaller is \(\boxed{17}\). The check is the original statement, \(17\cdot 18=306\).

review.x: Solve \(2x^2-338=0\). The common factor comes out first, and what remains is a difference of squares. Enter the negative root.
hints: Dividing out \(2\) leaves \(x^2-169=0\), a missing middle term with a negative square constant.
\(169=13^2\), so factor with the conjugate pair.
review.sol: Dividing out \(2\) gives \(x^2-169=(x+13)(x-13)=0\), so \(x=13\) or \(x=-13\), and the negative root is \(\boxed{-13}\). Checking, \(2\cdot 169-338=0\).

blocks.x: The quadratic \(2x^2+7x+3\) factors as \((2x+1)(x+3)\). Expand to check, \(2x^2+6x+x+3=2x^2+7x+3\). What is new is the leading term. \(2x^2\) is the product of the two leading terms, so the leading coefficient must also be split between the factors, and the middle coefficient depends on that split as well as on the constants.

Factor \(5x^2+29x+20\). Since \(5\) is prime, the leading terms can only be \(5x\) and \(x\), so the factorization has the shape \((5x+q)(x+s)\) with \(q\) and \(s\) positive whole numbers. Enter \(q\), the constant beside \(5x\).
hints: The leading split is forced, so only the two constants are unknown. List the positive factor pairs of \(20\), keeping both orders of each pair, since swapping the constants changes the middle term.
Check each candidate on its cross sum \(5s+q\), which must equal \(29\). The pair with \(q=20\) beside \(5x\) gives \(25\), close but wrong, so keep going.
blocks.sol: The cross sum \(5s+q\) must equal \(29\). Among the factor pairs of \(20\), the pair \(q=4\), \(s=5\) gives \(5\cdot 5+4=29\), so \(5x^2+29x+20=(5x+4)(x+5)\) and \(q=\boxed{4}\). The swapped order \(q=5\), \(s=4\) gives \(25\) instead, which is why each pair is checked in both orders.

blocks.x: Factor \(11x^2+39x-20\). The split of \(11\) is forced, so the shape is \((11x+q)(x+s)\). The product \(qs=-20\) is negative, so \(q\) and \(s\) have opposite signs. Enter the negative constant.
hints: The cross sum \(11s+q\) must equal \(+39\), a large positive number, so the positive term must be \(11s\). That makes \(s\) positive and \(q\) negative.
Test the factor pairs of \(20\) with \(s\) positive and \(q\) negative, checking the cross sum \(11s+q\) against \(39\) each time.
blocks.sol: With \(s\) positive and \(q\) negative, the pair \(q=-5\), \(s=4\) gives the cross sum \(11\cdot 4-5=39\), so \(11x^2+39x-20=(11x-5)(x+4)\) and the negative constant is \(\boxed{-5}\). Fixing the signs first cut the candidate list in half, since a cross sum as large as \(+39\) is out of reach when \(s\) is negative.

blocks.x: Three conditions. Distributing twice, \((px+q)(rx+s)=prx^2+psx+qrx+qs\). Matched against \(ax^2+bx+c\), three conditions are read off. The leading terms multiply to the leading coefficient, \(pr=a\). The constants multiply to the constant, \(qs=c\). The middle coefficient is the sum of the two cross products, \(ps+qr=b\). When \(a=1\) the split is \(p=r=1\) and the cross sum is just \(q+s\), 9.2's sum clue. For any other \(a\) the middle depends on how \(a\) is split, so a candidate is a choice of both pairs together, judged on its cross sum.

Factor \(25x^2+75x+54\). Now the leading terms can split as \(25x\) and \(x\) or as \(5x\) and \(5x\), and both splits have to be searched. Both constants are positive. Enter the larger of the two constants in the factorization.
hints: The constant pairs to test are \(1\cdot 54\), \(2\cdot 27\), \(3\cdot 18\) and \(6\cdot 9\), each one usable in either order. Check every candidate on its cross sum against \(75\).

In the \((25x+q)(x+s)\) rows the cross sum is \(25s+q\), and the smallest one those pairs give is \(77\), which is already above \(75\). In the \((5x+q)(5x+s)\) rows it is \(5(q+s)\), so \(q+s=15\) with \(qs=54\).
blocks.sol: Pairing the larger constant with \(25x\) gives cross sums \(79\), \(77\), \(93\) and \(159\), and swapping each pair only raises the sum, so the \(25x\) and \(x\) split is out. In the \((5x+q)(5x+s)\) split the cross sum is \(5(q+s)=75\), so \(q+s=15\) with \(qs=54\), and the pair is \(6\) and \(9\). So \(25x^2+75x+54=(5x+6)(5x+9)\) and the larger constant is \(\boxed{9}\). When the two leading terms are equal, the condition on the constants is exactly 9.2's sum and product search.

blocks.x: Every candidate for \(5x^2+53x+72\) has the shape \((5x+q)(x+s)\) with \(q\) and \(s\) positive and \(qs=72\), and counting order there are twelve such pairs. The middle coefficient \(53\) is odd. How many of the twelve candidates survive that one observation?
hints: The cross sum is \(5s+q\). Work out its parity when \(q\) and \(s\) are both even, using the fact that \(5s\) has the same parity as \(s\).
When \(q\) and \(s\) are both even the cross sum is even, and \(53\) is odd. Count the ordered pairs of \(72\) with both entries even, then subtract from twelve.
blocks.sol: Since \(5s\) has the parity of \(s\), the cross sum \(5s+q\) is even whenever \(q\) and \(s\) are both even, and an even sum cannot equal \(53\). Both odd is impossible, since \(qs=72\) is even. The all-even ordered pairs are \(2\cdot 36\), \(4\cdot 18\), \(6\cdot 12\) and their swaps, six in all, and removing them from the twelve leaves \(\boxed{6}\). One survivor checks, \(5\cdot 9+8=53\), so \(5x^2+53x+72=(5x+8)(x+9)\).

blocks.x: The organized search. List the factor pairs of \(a\) for the leading terms and the factor pairs of \(c\) for the constants. A candidate is one pair from each list and nothing else, and it passes only when its cross sum \(ps+qr\) equals \(b\). Both lists are finite, so the search finishes. 9.2's sign reasoning applies unchanged, and two more filters come from \(b\). An odd \(b\) is impossible when every entry is even, since both cross products would be even, and a small \(b\) is impossible when both cross products are large. Both filters cut candidates before any cross sum is worked out.

blocks.cap: The candidate check for \(ax^2+bx+c\). Stack the candidate factors, \(px+q\) over \(rx+s\). The left column product \(pr\) must equal \(a\), and the right column product \(qs\) must equal \(c\). The gold diagonals mark \(ps\) and \(qr\), and their sum must equal \(b\). Every candidate matches \(a\) and \(c\) by construction, so the middle term is the only place one can fail.

blocks.x: The first step has not changed. Before any lists get written, pull out the greatest common numeric factor and keep it in front. Sometimes what remains is monic, and the whole problem is back in 9.2's shorter search. Sometimes the remaining leading coefficient is smaller but still above \(1\), and both lists are shorter for it.
Factor \(30x^2-156x-144\) completely. Written as \(g(5x+q)(x+s)\), where \(g\) is the greatest common numeric factor, enter \(s\).
hints: All three coefficients are divisible by \(6\). Take the \(6\) out first. The quadratic that remains has leading coefficient \(5\), smaller but above \(1\), so a search is still needed.
Factor \(5x^2-26x-24\) as \((5x+q)(x+s)\). The constant is negative, so \(q\) and \(s\) have opposite signs, and the cross sum \(5s+q\) must equal \(-26\).
blocks.sol: The greatest common factor is \(6\), leaving \(6(5x^2-26x-24)\). The constant is negative, so \(q\) and \(s\) have opposite signs, and \(q=4\), \(s=-6\) gives the cross sum \(5(-6)+4=-26\), so \(30x^2-156x-144=6(5x+4)(x-6)\) and \(s=\boxed{-6}\). Taking the \(6\) out first made every number in the search smaller. The leading coefficient stayed above \(1\), so a search was still needed, just on easier numbers.

blocks.x: Factor \(81x^2-100\) into two binomials with integer coefficients. There is no middle term to search on, and both end terms are perfect squares, so this is one of 9.1's identities rather than a candidate list. The two constants are opposites. Enter the positive one.
hints: No candidate search is needed here. Expand \((9x+q)(9x-q)\) with the double distribution and see which terms cancel.
The expansion leaves \(81x^2-q^2\), so \(q^2=100\), and \(q\) is the positive choice.
blocks.sol: Since \(81x^2=(9x)^2\) and \(100=10^2\), the conjugate identity gives \(81x^2-100=(9x+10)(9x-10)\), so \(q=\boxed{10}\). Expanding, the cross products \(90x\) and \(-90x\) sum to zero, which is why the middle term is missing.

blocks.x: Common factor first, then identities. After the numeric factor is out, check the two identity shapes before writing any lists. Both of 9.1's identities apply with \(ax\) as the first term. A difference of two perfect square terms is a conjugate product, \(9x^2-49=(3x)^2-7^2=(3x+7)(3x-7)\). A trinomial whose end terms are perfect squares, with a middle term twice the product of their roots, is a perfect square, \(25x^2+30x+9=(5x+3)^2\), since \(2\cdot 5x\cdot 3=30x\). A quadratic recognized this way is factored on sight, with no candidate list at all.

An empty search is still a proof. In \(3x^2+4x+5\) the only leading split is \(3x\) and \(x\), and the constants must be the positive pair \(1\) and \(5\). \((3x+1)(x+5)\) has cross sum \(16x\), \((3x+5)(x+1)\) has cross sum \(8x\), neither is \(4x\), and no integer factorization exists. Quadratics like this are handled in chapter 11.
Does \(4x^2+13x+6\) factor into two binomials with integer coefficients? Run the full search, every leading split against every constant pair, before answering yes or no.
hints: Both constants have to be positive, since their product \(6\) and the middle coefficient \(13\) are both positive. Then \(4\) splits only as \(4\cdot 1\) or \(2\cdot 2\), so the whole list has six candidates.
The middle coefficient \(13\) is odd, so a candidate whose two cross products are both even is impossible. That removes the \((2x+q)(2x+s)\) row, and checking the rest settles it.
blocks.sol: The \((4x+q)(x+s)\) row has cross sums \(25\), \(10\), \(14\), \(11\) for \((q,s)=(1,6)\), \((6,1)\), \((2,3)\), \((3,2)\), and the \((2x+q)(2x+s)\) row has \(14\) and \(10\). Both constants had to be positive and \(4\) splits only as \(4\cdot 1\) or \(2\cdot 2\), so those six are the whole list, and none has cross sum \(13\), making the answer \(\boxed{\text{no}}\).

blocks.x: Emmy Noether's 1921 paper turned factoring itself into a subject. It asked in which number systems every factorization is unique, not how to factor one expression, and much of modern algebra descends from it.
Solve \(4x^2+27x-40=0\). Factor the left side, then split with the zero product property. Enter the positive root, as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The leading \(4\) splits as \(4\cdot 1\) or \(2\cdot 2\), and a \(2x\) paired with \(2x\) always has an even cross sum, while \(27\) is odd.

So the factors have the form \((4x+q)(x+s)\), with \(qs=-40\) and cross sum \(4s+q=27\). The constant is negative, so \(q\) and \(s\) have opposite signs. Once the factoring is done, set each factor equal to zero on its own.
blocks.sol: The left side factors as \(4x^2+27x-40=(4x-5)(x+8)\), since the cross products \(32x\) and \(-5x\) add to \(27x\). By the zero product property either \(4x-5=0\) or \(x+8=0\), so the roots are \(\tfrac{5}{4}\) and \(-8\), and the positive root is \(\boxed{\tfrac{5}{4}}\). The root is a fraction because \(4x-5=0\) is finished by dividing by \(4\).

blocks.x: Fraction roots. By the zero product property, each factor set to zero is a linear equation, and \(px+q=0\) gives \(x=-\tfrac{q}{p}\), the constant with its sign flipped, divided by the coefficient of \(x\). In 9.2 every factor was \(x+q\), so every root was an integer. With the leading coefficient split between the factors, a root is a fraction whenever \(p\) does not divide \(q\), and that is normal, not a sign of error. Write every fraction root exactly and in lowest terms. Reading the root off a factor without the sign flip, or without the division by \(p\), is the standard mistake.

The zero product property applies to a product equal to zero and nothing else, so the first move has not changed. When a quadratic equation has terms on both sides, subtract until one side is zero, collect like terms, and only then factor and split. A factored left side proves nothing while the right side is nonzero.

Solve \(5x^2+22x=48\). The right side is not zero, and the zero product property applies only to a product that equals zero, so rearrange first, then factor and split. Enter the positive root as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Move \(48\) across so the right side is zero. The leading coefficient \(5\) is prime, so the split of the leading terms is forced.
Search \((5x+q)(x+s)\) with \(qs=-48\), and keep the candidate whose cross products add to \(22x\).
blocks.sol: Moving \(48\) across gives \(5x^2+22x-48=0\). Since \(5\) is prime the leading terms split as \(5x\) and \(x\), and \(-8\) with \(6\) gives cross products \(30x\) and \(-8x\), which add to \(22x\), so \(5x^2+22x-48=(5x-8)(x+6)\). Then \(5x-8=0\) or \(x+6=0\), so \(x=\tfrac{8}{5}\) or \(x=-6\), and the positive root is \(\boxed{\tfrac{8}{5}}\). Checking in the original equation, \(5\cdot\tfrac{64}{25}+22\cdot\tfrac{8}{5}=\tfrac{64}{5}+\tfrac{176}{5}=48\).

blocks.x: The first and last terms of \(144x^2+bx+49\) are both perfect squares. Find the positive value of \(b\) that makes the whole trinomial the square of a binomial.
hints: Start by writing those two terms as squares, \(144x^2=(12x)^2\) and \(49=7^2\).
Expanding \((px+q)^2\) gives \(p^2x^2+2pqx+q^2\), so the middle coefficient is twice the product of the two terms being squared, not just their product.
blocks.sol: The first and last terms are \((12x)^2\) and \(7^2\), and with \(b\) positive the trinomial is \((12x+7)^2=144x^2+168x+49\), so \(b=\boxed{168}\). A common slip is \(84\), the product \(12\cdot 7\) without the doubling. The middle term of a square is twice that product, one copy from each cross product.

blocks.x: The full pipeline, extended. Rearrange until one side is zero. Pull out the common numeric factor, and \(x\) itself when there is no constant term. Check for a difference of squares or a perfect square with \(ax\) as the first term. Otherwise run the organized search, signs first, then the parity and size of \(b\), then cross sums. Split with the zero product property and reduce every fraction root to lowest terms. That is 9.2's pipeline with one new layer, the split of the leading coefficient. Put a fraction root back into the original equation, since a slip in the split shows up there at once.

You can now take any quadratic with integer coefficients through one finite process, common factor out, identities checked, candidates listed, narrowed, and tested on their cross sums. When an integer factorization exists the process ends on it, and an exhausted list is a proof that none exists. The two closing problems draw on most of it at once.

Factor \(24x^2-34x-45\) into two binomials with integer coefficients, writing both leading coefficients as positive. Since the constant is \(-45\), the two constants in the factors have opposite signs, so exactly one of them is negative. Enter that negative constant.
hints: Both constants in the factors are odd, since their product is \(-45\). The cross products must add to the even number \(-34\), and that happens only when the two leading coefficients have the same parity.
Try the split \(4\cdot 6\) of \(24\) against the odd factor pairs of \(45\), with signs chosen so the cross products add to \(-34\).
blocks.sol: Both constants are odd, since their product is \(-45\), so each cross product has the parity of its leading coefficient, and those add to the even \(-34\). Both leading coefficients are therefore even, leaving the splits \(2\cdot 12\) and \(4\cdot 6\) of \(24\). No odd pair of \(45\) fits \(2\cdot 12\), and \(4\cdot 6\) with constants \(-9\) and \(5\) gives cross products \(-54x\) and \(20x\), so \(24x^2-34x-45=(4x-9)(6x+5)\) and the negative constant is \(\boxed{-9}\). With an odd constant and an even middle coefficient, only the even splits of \(a\) are possible, which is a fast first cut.

blocks.x: Solve \(36x^2+13x-40=0\). There are five splits of \(36\) and four factor pairs of \(40\), so narrow the list with sign and parity reasoning before trying candidates. Enter the negative root as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The middle coefficient \(13\) is odd, so one cross product is odd and one is even. An all even split of \(36\) or an all even factor pair of \(40\) makes both of them even.

After the parity cut the splits still open are \(1\cdot 36\), \(3\cdot 12\), \(4\cdot 9\) and the pairs \(1\cdot 40\), \(5\cdot 8\). The constant is negative, so the two cross product sizes differ by \(13\).
blocks.sol: Factoring gives \(36x^2+13x-40=(4x+5)(9x-8)\), so \(4x+5=0\) or \(9x-8=0\), and the roots are \(x=-\tfrac{5}{4}\) and \(x=\tfrac{8}{9}\), making the negative root \(\boxed{-\tfrac{5}{4}}\). The search is short because \(13\) is odd, which rules out every all even split of \(36\) and every all even factor pair of \(40\).

blocks.x: So far every root in this chapter was found the same way, factor first, then read each root off its factor. Lesson 9.4, Roots, Sums, and Products, works without that step. The sum and the product of a quadratic's roots can be read straight from its coefficients, so questions about the roots can be answered without ever finding them. That is new.

review.x: Factor \(5x^2+31x+44\). The leading coefficient is prime, so the two factors can only begin with \(5x\) and \(x\). Enter the constant in the factor whose leading term is \(5x\).
hints: With the leading split forced, the shape is \((5x+q)(x+s)\) and the cross sum is \(5s+q\), which must equal \(31\).
Both constants are positive and \(qs=44\). Test the pairs of \(44\) in both orders, since swapping them changes the cross sum.
review.sol: The shape is \((5x+q)(x+s)\) with \(qs=44\) and cross sum \(5s+q=31\). The pair \(q=11\), \(s=4\) gives \(5\cdot 4+11=31\), so \(5x^2+31x+44=(5x+11)(x+4)\) and the constant beside \(5x\) is \(\boxed{11}\). The swapped order \(q=4\), \(s=11\) gives \(59\), which is why order matters.

review.x: Factor \(11x^2-38x-24\). The leading coefficient is prime, so the linear terms can only be \(11x\) and \(x\). Enter the negative one of the two constants in the factored form.
hints: The constant term is negative, so one constant is positive and one is negative, with product \(-24\).
Expanding \((11x+q)(x+s)\) gives middle coefficient \(11s+q\). With \(qs=-24\), try \(s\) negative and \(q\) positive first.
review.sol: In \((11x+q)(x+s)\) with \(qs=-24\), the middle coefficient is \(11s+q\), and \(s=-4\) with \(q=6\) gives \(-44+6=-38\). So \(11x^2-38x-24=(11x+6)(x-4)\), and the negative constant is \(\boxed{-4}\). Flipping both signs gives \((11x-6)(x+4)\), whose middle coefficient is \(+38\), the right size and the wrong sign.

review.x: Factor \(6x^2+41x+30\) into two binomials with positive integer coefficients. The leading coefficient is not prime, so there is more than one way to split it between the two factors. Enter the smaller of the two constants.
hints: Both constants are positive and multiply to \(30\). The leading coefficient splits as \(2\cdot 3\) or as \(6\cdot 1\), so there are two shapes to try.
For \((2x+q)(3x+s)\) the middle coefficient is \(2s+3q\), and for \((6x+q)(x+s)\) it is \(6s+q\). Run the factor pairs of \(30\) through both until one gives \(41\).
review.sol: Splitting the leading coefficient as \(6\cdot 1\) gives \(6x^2+41x+30=(6x+5)(x+6)\), with middle coefficient \(6\cdot 6+5=41\) and constants multiplying to \(30\), so the smaller constant is \(\boxed{5}\). The balanced split \((2x+q)(3x+s)\) is a dead end, since no factor pair of \(30\) makes \(2s+3q=41\).

review.x: Factor \(9x^2-31x-70\) into two binomials with integer coefficients. The middle coefficient is not a multiple of \(3\), which rules out the split with \(3x\) in both factors, since that split makes every cross sum a multiple of \(3\). Enter the positive constant.
hints: With the \(3x\) split ruled out, the shape is \((9x+q)(x+s)\) and the cross sum is \(9s+q\), which must equal \(-31\).
The constant \(-70\) is negative, so \(q\) and \(s\) have opposite signs, and the cross sum is negative, so the larger cross product is the negative one.
review.sol: In the \((3x+q)(3x+s)\) split every cross sum is \(3(q+s)\), a multiple of \(3\), and \(-31\) is not, so the shape is \((9x+q)(x+s)\) with \(9s+q=-31\) and \(qs=-70\). The pair \(q=14\), \(s=-5\) gives \(9(-5)+14=-31\), so \(9x^2-31x-70=(9x+14)(x-5)\) and the positive constant is \(\boxed{14}\). Ruling out a whole split by divisibility is cheaper than testing its rows one at a time.

review.x: Factor \(4x^2+31x+60\). The middle coefficient is odd, so the two factors cannot both have an even coefficient on \(x\), since both cross products would then be even. Enter the constant in the factor whose leading term is \(4x\).
hints: That rules out splitting \(4x^2\) as \(2x\) times \(2x\), so the linear terms are \(4x\) and \(x\). Every term is positive, so both constants are positive with product \(60\).
Expanding \((4x+q)(x+s)\) gives middle coefficient \(4s+q\). Try the positive pairs with \(qs=60\) in both orders and find the one with \(4s+q=31\).
review.sol: The all-even split is out, so the linear terms are \(4x\) and \(x\). In \((4x+q)(x+s)\) with \(qs=60\), the middle coefficient is \(4s+q\), and \(q=15\) with \(s=4\) gives \(16+15=31\). So \(4x^2+31x+60=(4x+15)(x+4)\), and the constant asked for is \(\boxed{15}\). Checking parity first rules out the \(2x\) times \(2x\) split before any candidate is expanded.

review.x: Factor \(5x^2+60x+160\) completely, pulling out the greatest common numeric factor before any candidate search. Enter the larger of the two constants in the binomials that remain.
hints: All three coefficients share a numeric factor. Divide it out and look at the leading coefficient of what is left.
What remains is monic, so no candidate search is needed. Find the pair with sum \(12\) and product \(32\).
review.sol: Every coefficient is a multiple of \(5\), so \(5x^2+60x+160=5(x^2+12x+32)\). The pair with sum \(12\) and product \(32\) is \(4\) and \(8\), giving \(5(x+4)(x+8)\), so the larger constant is \(\boxed{8}\). Pulling the \(5\) out first leaves a monic quadratic, so the sum and product search finishes it with no candidate list to check.

review.x: Each end term of \(196x^2-169\) is a perfect square and there is no middle term, so this is the conjugate identity rather than a search. Factor it as \((14x+q)(14x-q)\) with \(q\) positive. What is \(q\)?
hints: The identity is \(a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)\), and here \(a=14x\), since \((14x)^2=196x^2\).
The second term is \(b^2=169\), so \(b\) is the number whose square is \(169\).
review.sol: Since \(196x^2=(14x)^2\) and \(169=13^2\), the identity gives \(196x^2-169=(14x+13)(14x-13)\), so \(q=\boxed{13}\). The two cross products are \(-182x\) and \(+182x\), which cancel, and that cancellation is why the middle term is missing.

review.x: Does \(6x^2+5x+4\) factor into two binomials with integer coefficients? Both the constant and the middle coefficient are positive, so both constants would have to be positive. Run every leading split against every constant pair before answering yes or no.
hints: The leading coefficient splits as \(6\cdot 1\) or \(2\cdot 3\), and the positive factor pairs of \(4\) are \(1\cdot 4\), \(2\cdot 2\) and \(4\cdot 1\).
Work out the cross sum for each of the six candidates and compare every one against \(5\). The smallest cross sum any candidate reaches is well above it.
review.sol: For \((6x+q)(x+s)\) the cross sum \(6s+q\) gives \(25\), \(14\) and \(10\), and for \((2x+q)(3x+s)\) the cross sum \(2s+3q\) gives \(11\), \(10\) and \(14\). None of the six equals \(5\), so the answer is \(\boxed{\text{no}}\). The search is finite, so coming up empty is a complete answer, and quadratics like this one get their treatment in chapter 11.

review.x: Factor \(6x^2-17x-114\) as \((6x+q)(x+s)\) with integers \(q\) and \(s\). The constant term is negative, so \(q\) and \(s\) have opposite signs. Enter \(q\).
hints: Expanding \((6x+q)(x+s)\) gives the two conditions \(qs=-114\) and \(6s+q=-17\).
The factor pairs of \(114\) are \(1\cdot 114\), \(2\cdot 57\), \(3\cdot 38\) and \(6\cdot 19\). Each pair has to be tried in both slots, since \(6\) multiplies \(s\) and not \(q\).
review.sol: The conditions are \(qs=-114\) and \(6s+q=-17\). Among the factor pairs of \(114\), only \(6\) and \(19\) fit, with \(s=-6\) and \(q=19\) giving \(6(-6)+19=-17\), so \(6x^2-17x-114=(6x+19)(x-6)\) and \(q=\boxed{19}\). The order inside the pair matters, since \(s=-19\) with \(q=6\) gives \(6(-19)+6=-108\) instead.

review.x: Factor \(4x^2+9x-100\) as \((4x+q)(x+s)\) with integers \(q\) and \(s\). The constant is large while the middle coefficient is small, so the two cross products very nearly cancel. Enter \(q\).
hints: The conditions are \(qs=-100\) and \(4s+q=9\). Since the product is negative, \(q\) and \(s\) have opposite signs.
Start with \(s\) negative and \(q\) positive, and run the factor pairs of \(100\). The sum \(4s+q\) gets smaller as \(|s|\) grows, so begin at \(s=-1\) and work down.
review.sol: The conditions are \(qs=-100\) and \(4s+q=9\). The pair \(s=-4\), \(q=25\) meets both, since \(25\cdot(-4)=-100\) and \(4(-4)+25=9\), so \(4x^2+9x-100=(4x+25)(x-4)\) and \(q=\boxed{25}\). A \(2\cdot 2\) split of the leading coefficient is impossible here, since \((2x+m)(2x+n)\) has even middle coefficient \(2m+2n\) while \(9\) is odd.

review.x: Each end term of \(25x^2-kx+81\) is a perfect square. There is exactly one positive number \(k\) that makes the whole quadratic the square of a binomial. What is \(k\)?
hints: If \(25x^2-kx+81=(ax-b)^2\), then \(a^2=25\) and \(b^2=81\), and expanding gives the middle term \(-2abx\), so \(k=2ab\).
The middle term of a squared binomial is twice the product of its two terms, so compare \(kx\) against that.
review.sol: The end terms are \((5x)^2\) and \(9^2\), and \((5x-9)^2=25x^2-90x+81\), so \(k=\boxed{90}\). The middle term of a squared binomial is twice the product of the two terms being squared, so its size here is \(2\cdot 5\cdot 9=90\), and it is negative because of the minus in \(5x-9\).

review.x: Solve \(9x^2+16x-80=0\). One root is negative and one is a positive fraction. Enter the positive root as an exact fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Factor first. The form \((9x+q)(x+s)\) needs \(qs=-80\) and cross sum \(9s+q=16\).
The constant is negative, so the two constants in the factors have opposite signs, and the cross sum must come out to \(16\).
review.sol: The conditions \(qs=-80\) and \(9s+q=16\) hold for \(q=-20\), \(s=4\), so \(9x^2+16x-80=(9x-20)(x+4)\). The zero product property gives \(9x-20=0\) or \(x+4=0\), so \(x=\tfrac{20}{9}\) or \(x=-4\), and the positive root is \(x=\boxed{\tfrac{20}{9}}\). Checking the middle term, \(36x-20x=16x\).

review.x: Solve \(20x^2+45x-275=0\). A numeric factor comes out of all three terms first, and what remains still has a leading coefficient above \(1\). Enter the positive root as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Every coefficient is divisible by \(5\). Take that factor out first so the search that remains is smaller.
Factor \(4x^2+9x-55\) as \((4x+q)(x+s)\), cross sum \(4s+q=9\) with \(qs=-55\).
review.sol: Dividing by \(5\) leaves \(4x^2+9x-55=0\). A \(2x\) times \(2x\) split would make the middle coefficient even, so the leading terms are \(4x\) and \(x\), and \((4x-11)(x+5)\) has cross sum \(20-11=9\) with constant \(-55\). The roots of \(5(4x-11)(x+5)=0\) are \(\tfrac{11}{4}\) and \(-5\), so the positive root is \(\boxed{\tfrac{11}{4}}\). The factor \(5\) is never zero, so only the binomials give roots.

review.x: Factor \(20x^2-89x+80\) into two binomials with integer coefficients. Enter the constant in the factor whose leading term is \(5x\), sign included.
hints: Both constants are negative, and \(89\) is odd, so no candidate with two even constants can work. \(80\) has very few odd divisors.
The named leading term pins the split to \((4x+q)(5x+s)\), so \(qs=80\) and the cross sum \(4s+5q\) must be \(-89\).
review.sol: The split \((4x+q)(5x+s)\) needs \(qs=80\) and \(4s+5q=-89\). The pair \(q=-5\), \(s=-16\) fits, since \(4(-16)+5(-5)=-64-25=-89\), so \(20x^2-89x+80=(4x-5)(5x-16)\) and the constant in the \(5x\) factor is \(\boxed{-16}\). An odd middle coefficient needs one odd constant, and the only odd divisors of \(80\) are \(1\) and \(5\), so only two candidates ever need checking.

review.x: Factor \(36x^2-60x-119\) into two binomials with integer coefficients, writing both leading coefficients as positive. The constant is negative, so exactly one of the two constants in the factors is negative. Enter that negative constant.
hints: The constant \(-119\) has only two factor pairs, so the constant side of the candidate list is short. Work both out before listing the splits of \(36\).
One split of \(36\) is \(6\cdot 6\). In \((6x+q)(6x+s)\) the cross sum is \(6(q+s)\), which is divisible by \(6\), and so is \(-60\).
review.sol: With the split \(6\cdot 6\) the cross sum is \(6(q+s)=-60\), giving \(q+s=-10\) with \(qs=-119\), which is the pair \(7\) and \(-17\). Then \(36x^2-60x-119=(6x+7)(6x-17)\) and the negative constant is \(\boxed{-17}\). A middle coefficient divisible by \(6\) makes the split with two equal leading terms worth trying first, since equal leading terms make the cross sum a multiple of them.

review.x: Solve \(20x^2+51x-90=0\). Neither root is a whole number here, which is ordinary once the leading coefficient is above \(1\). Enter the positive root as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The leading \(20\) splits as \(1\cdot 20\), \(2\cdot 10\), or \(4\cdot 5\). With \(2\) and \(10\) both cross products are even, so that split cannot reach the odd middle \(51\).
Try the split \((5x+q)(4x+s)\), where \(qs=-90\) and the cross sum \(5s+4q\) must be \(51\).
review.sol: The split \((5x+q)(4x+s)\) with \(q=-6\) and \(s=15\) has cross sum \(5\cdot 15+4\cdot(-6)=51\), so \((5x-6)(4x+15)=0\) and the roots are \(\tfrac{6}{5}\) and \(-\tfrac{15}{4}\), with positive root \(\boxed{\tfrac{6}{5}}\). The root from \(5x-6=0\) is \(\tfrac{6}{5}\), not \(-\tfrac{6}{5}\), since \(5x=6\).

review.x: Solve \(48x^2+26x=55\). The right side is not zero, and the zero product property needs it to be, so rearrange before factoring. Enter the negative root as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Rearrange to \(48x^2+26x-55=0\) first. The constant is negative, so the factor constants differ in sign.
Among the splits of \(48\), try \((8x+q)(6x+s)\), cross sum \(8s+6q=26\) with \(qs=-55\).
review.sol: Rearranged, \(48x^2+26x-55=0\). The split \((8x+q)(6x+s)\) with \(q=11\), \(s=-5\) gives \(8(-5)+6\cdot 11=26\), so \((8x+11)(6x-5)=0\) with roots \(-\tfrac{11}{8}\) and \(\tfrac{5}{6}\). The negative root is \(\boxed{-\tfrac{11}{8}}\). Each factor \(px+q\) contributes the root \(-q/p\), so a leading coefficient that does not divide its constant leaves a fraction.

blocks.x: A monic quadratic with roots \(r\) and \(s\) factors as \((x-r)(x-s)\), 9.2's factorization written with the roots rather than the search numbers. Expanding gives \(x^2-(r+s)x+rs\). Against \(x^2+bx+c\), \(b=-(r+s)\) and \(c=rs\), so the roots add to \(-b\) and multiply to \(c\). In \(x^2-10x+21=(x-3)(x-7)\) the roots add to \(10\) and multiply to \(21\).
The roots of \(x^2-17x+52\) are \(r\) and \(s\). Find \(r+s\) without factoring the quadratic and without finding either root.
hints: Multiply \((x-r)(x-s)\) out. The coefficient of \(x\) in the expansion is \(-(r+s)\).
Match that against the coefficient of \(x\) in \(x^2-17x+52\), which is \(-17\) with its sign, and solve for \(r+s\).
blocks.sol: Expanding, \((x-r)(x-s)=x^2-(r+s)x+rs\), and matching the middle coefficients gives \(-(r+s)=-17\), so \(r+s=\boxed{17}\). Watch the sign, the coefficient of \(x\) is \(-17\), so the sum is its opposite and not \(-17\) itself.

blocks.x: The roots of \(x^2+6x-91\) are \(r\) and \(s\). Match the quadratic against \((x-r)(x-s)\) expanded and read off the product \(rs\). Enter it as an integer.
hints: Match \(x^2+6x-91\) against the expanded form \((x-r)(x-s)=x^2-(r+s)x+rs\). The product of the roots sits in the constant slot.
For a second route, factor the quadratic into two whole-number factors, read a root off each factor, and multiply the two roots.
blocks.sol: Matching \(x^2+6x-91\) with \((x-r)(x-s)=x^2-(r+s)x+rs\) puts the product in the constant slot, so \(rs=\boxed{-91}\). In \(x^2-(r+s)x+rs\) the sign flip is on the sum term only, so the constant is the product with no change. Factoring gives \((x+13)(x-7)\), so the roots are \(-13\) and \(7\), and \(-13\cdot 7=-91\).

blocks.x: Sum and product of the roots. If \(x^2+bx+c\) has roots \(r\) and \(s\), it equals \((x-r)(x-s)=x^2-(r+s)x+rs\), so \(r+s=-b\) and \(rs=c\). The sign on the sum is the part that gets misread. In 9.2 the same two letters stood for the search numbers, the constants inside \((x+r)(x+s)\), and that product is zero at \(-r\) and \(-s\), not at \(r\) and \(s\). So 9.2's search numbers are the negatives of the roots. The search numbers add to \(b\), and the roots add to \(-b\).
The numbers \(6\) and \(17\) multiply to \(102\) and add to \(23\), so \(x^2+23x+102=(x+6)(x+17)\). What is the sum of the two roots?
hints: The two numbers given are the constants inside the factors. A root is a value of \(x\) that makes a factor zero, which is a different thing.
\(x+6\) is zero at \(x=-6\), so the roots are \(-6\) and \(-17\). Add those, or read \(-b\) straight off the quadratic.
blocks.sol: The sum of the roots is \(-b\), so \(r+s=\boxed{-23}\). The factors are \(x+6\) and \(x+17\), and \(x+6\) is zero at \(-6\), not at \(6\), so the roots are \(-6\) and \(-17\), which add to \(-23\). Adding the two search numbers instead gives \(23\), the right size with the wrong sign.

blocks.x: The quadratic \(8x^2+18x-5\) factors as \((2x+5)(4x-1)\). Find its two roots and add them. Enter the sum as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Each factor is zero at one root. Set \(2x+5=0\) and \(4x-1=0\), and solve each one.
The roots are \(-\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\). Put both over the denominator \(4\) before adding.
blocks.sol: From \((2x+5)(4x-1)\) the roots are \(-\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\), so the sum is \(-\frac{10}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=\boxed{-\frac{9}{4}}\). That is \(-\frac{18}{8}\) reduced, the middle coefficient over the leading one with the sign flipped, which is not a coincidence.

blocks.x: Any leading coefficient. Divide \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) through by \(a\), which is not zero, and what remains is \(x^2+\frac{b}{a}x+\frac{c}{a}=0\). Dividing both sides of an equation by a nonzero number changes no solution, so this quadratic has the same two roots, and the monic rule applies to it as written. Then \(r+s=-\frac{b}{a}\) and \(rs=\frac{c}{a}\). The last problem is the check. For \(8x^2+18x-5\) the sum is \(-\frac{18}{8}=-\frac{9}{4}\) and the product is \(-\frac{5}{8}\). When \(a=1\) these are \(-b\) and \(c\) again.
